FHSA over-contribution: the 1% tax on the highest excess each month, what a designated withdrawal can and cannot fix, and how the excess eats next year’s room

Follow the Income Tax Act’s excess FHSA amount month by month: why there is no cushion, why removing the excess still leaves that month taxed, why a designated withdrawal cannot get ahead of payroll contributions, how a taxable withdrawal creates re-participation room, and how an excess left in December reduces the next January’s room. Uses CRA’s FHSA statistics for 2024.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 10 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

The central idea

A first home savings account (FHSA) has no over-contribution cushion. Any contributions and RRSP transfers above your participation room, across all your FHSAs, are an excess FHSA amount, taxed at 1% of the highest excess at any time in each month. Withdrawing it stops the tax from the next month, not the current one. A designated withdrawal (Form RC727) is tax-free but limited to the excess at that moment, so it cannot get ahead of payroll contributions that are still coming. An excess left at year-end is absorbed by the next January’s room, which leaves less room for that year. In 2024 FHSA holders had 225,210 more accounts than people.

01

How an FHSA excess starts

The first home savings account (FHSA) gives each eligible first-time buyer CAD 8,000 of participation room a year, up to CAD 40,000 in a lifetime, with up to CAD 8,000 of unused room carried into the next year. The room belongs to the person, not the account. Most excesses come from that detail: a payroll plan at one institution keeps contributing after a lump sum or an RRSP transfer has gone into an FHSA at another; carried-forward room is counted twice; or a holder assumes that a withdrawal gives room back, as it does for a TFSA the following year.

The calculator follows a single person through 2026 and 2027 with a monthly contribution, one lump sum or RRSP transfer, one withdrawal and the new room that arrives on 1 January 2027. It answers four questions: when does the excess start, how much does a withdrawal save and in which month, which kind of withdrawal to use, and how much room is left for next year.

02

The excess FHSA amount and its tax, in the Act’s terms

Section 207.01(1) of the Income Tax Act defines the excess FHSA amount at any time in a year as A + B + C − D − E − F:

ElementMeaningIn the calculator
AThe excess at the end of last year (nil before the first year with an FHSA)Carried from December 2026 into 2027
B + CContributions, and transfers from an RRSP, made in the year so farMonthly and one-time amounts
DThe year’s room: CAD 8,000 plus the carryforward, but no more than CAD 40,000 less earlier amounts2026 room entered; 2027 room calculated
EDesignated amounts, and taxable withdrawals to the extent they reduce the excess, in the year so farThe withdrawal, by kind
FEarlier income inclusions not already used to reduce an excessTaken as nil

Section 207.021 then charges, for each month in which there is an excess at any time, 1% of the highest such amount in that month. Three consequences follow:

  • No cushion. An RRSP allows CAD 2,000 over the limit before tax applies; an FHSA allows nothing. The first dollar over room is taxed.
  • The month of the fix is still taxed. The test is the highest amount at any time in the month, as for a TFSA. Removing the excess on the 28th still leaves that month’s 1%; it stops the tax from the next month. Under the RRSP rule, which uses the month-end, the same withdrawal would avoid the month.
  • The excess does not lapse. It carries into the next year as element A and is absorbed only by that year’s new room or by a withdrawal.

03

Five worked cases

All use the calculator’s default: an FHSA opened in 2025 with CAD 3,000 contributed, which gives CAD 13,000 of room for 2026 (CAD 8,000 plus CAD 5,000 carried forward); CAD 500 a month by payroll at one institution through 2026; CAD 10,000 put into a second FHSA at another institution in April; and CAD 500 a month in 2027. Contributions reach CAD 13,000 in June and the excess starts in July.

  1. Nothing withdrawn. The highest excess is CAD 500 in July, rising by CAD 500 a month to CAD 3,000 in December: 1% of the total CAD 10,500 is CAD 105 for 2026. On 1 January 2027 the CAD 3,000 still over is absorbed by the CAD 8,000 of new room, leaving CAD 5,000; at CAD 500 a month that runs out in October 2027, and November and December cost another CAD 15. Total CAD 120.
  2. CAD 2,000 designated and withdrawn in October (the default). October is still taxed on its CAD 2,000 high point, and payroll rebuilds CAD 500 and CAD 1,000 in November and December: CAD 65 for 2026. The CAD 1,000 left in December uses part of 2027’s new room, leaving CAD 7,000, and 2027 stays within it.
  3. The best single month. Designating the whole excess in July, August, September, October, November or December gives CAD 85, 65, 60, 65, 80 and 105. Early withdrawals are small because the excess is small, and payroll recreates it; late ones come after months of tax. September is the cheapest here, but stopping the payroll contributions in July would beat every one of them.
  4. A taxable withdrawal of CAD 5,000 in October. The first CAD 2,000 reduces the excess, so the excess tax is the same CAD 65. The full CAD 5,000 is income, about CAD 1,500 at a 30% marginal rate, and the CAD 3,000 above the excess becomes re-participation room: 2027 room is CAD 10,000 after the CAD 1,000 carried in.
  5. CRA’s own examples. With the inputs set to them, the calculator reproduces the five checked cases on CRA’s pages: CAD 10,000 contributed in November against CAD 8,000 of room costs CAD 40 and leaves CAD 6,000 of room the next year; CAD 13,000 leaves CAD 3,000; a CAD 5,000 taxable withdrawal of a CAD 2,000 excess leaves CAD 11,000; a CAD 7,500 taxable withdrawal of a CAD 6,000 excess leaves CAD 9,500; and a CAD 1,500 excess removed the next month costs two months, CAD 30.

04

Designated or taxable: two ways out

CRA’s excess FHSA amounts page lists the ways an excess is reduced: new participation room on 1 January, a designated withdrawal, a designated transfer to an RRSP or RRIF, a taxable withdrawal, or income deemed received when the FHSA ceases.

Designated withdrawal (Form RC727)Taxable withdrawal
Income taxNot included in incomeThe whole amount is income for the year
MaximumThe excess at the time, and no more than your contributions less earlier designated withdrawalsAny amount in the account
Effect on the excessReduces it by the amountReduces it by up to the excess
Room afterwardsRestores that much of the CAD 40,000 lifetime limit; no new annual roomThe part above the excess becomes re-participation room next year

If the excess came from an RRSP transfer, a designated transfer back to an RRSP or RRIF is the counterpart of a designated withdrawal; it is not income and does not affect RRSP deduction room. Someone who only contributed can only make a designated withdrawal, and someone who only transferred can only make a designated transfer. The calculator treats contributions and transfers alike and models the withdrawal route.

Because the designated amount cannot exceed the excess when it is designated, it is a correction, not a reserve. The contributions that are still scheduled have to be stopped or reduced, or the excess comes back the next month, as the third chart shows.

05

What 1 January does, and what it costs

CRA says an excess is reduced or eliminated by your new participation room on 1 January of the following year. That ends the tax without a withdrawal, but it is not free:

  • The excess uses next year’s room. CRA’s example of a CAD 2,000 excess at the end of 2025 leaves CAD 6,000 of room for 2026, not CAD 8,000.
  • No carryforward is created. A year that ends over room has no unused room to carry forward, so the next year’s room is CAD 8,000 at most before the excess is subtracted.
  • The lifetime limit still counts the money. Contributions above room count against the CAD 40,000 until they are designated out.
  • Months of 1% tax run first. In the default case, waiting costs CAD 120 over two years against CAD 65 for a designated withdrawal in October.

CRA’s participation room page distinguishes the participation room carryforward, used for room and excess calculations, from the FHSA carryforward in section 146.6(1), used for the annual FHSA limit and deductions. They are equal in simple cases like these.

06

What CRA’s 2024 statistics show

CRA’s First Home Savings Account Statistics for the 2024 tax year, built from T4FHSA slips filed by financial institutions and processed to 30 June 2026, count 1,455,280 holders with 1,680,490 accounts: 1.155 accounts per holder. Room is shared across a person’s FHSAs, so each extra account is another place a contribution can be made without the first institution knowing.

Averages are total contributions divided by holders who contributed; CRA rounds counts to the nearest 10 and dollars to the nearest thousand. 2024 was the second year of the FHSA, the first in which carried-forward room let a holder put in more than CAD 8,000, and the two highest brackets averaged above it. Statistics Canada’s table for 2023, the first year, reports 484,320 contributors with a median of exactly CAD 8,000: many people contribute at the limit, where one extra deposit is an excess. Neither source counts excess amounts, so these figures describe exposure, not the number of people taxed.

07

If you are already over

  1. Add up every FHSA. Room is per person, so list contributions and transfers at every institution against the room on your notice of assessment or CRA account.
  2. Stop or reduce scheduled contributions until 1 January, or the excess returns.
  3. Ask each issuer for a designated withdrawal (or a designated transfer, if the excess came from an RRSP) on Form RC727, for no more than the excess at the time. Do it as early in a month as you can: the current month is taxed either way, and every further month adds 1%.
  4. File Form RC728 with Schedule A and pay by 30 June of the following year: by 30 June 2027 for an excess in 2026. CRA’s FHSA taxes page says a penalty and interest apply if you file late.
  5. Ask for a waiver if it was a reasonable error. CRA’s form for this tax is RC729, Request for Waiver or Cancellation of Tax on your Excess FHSA Amount, sent with FHSA statements showing when the excess arose and when it was removed. Penalties and interest go through Form RC4288 instead.

08

What the calculator leaves out

  • Growth. Amounts are contributions, not market values. Investment income does not use room, so an account worth more than you put in does not by itself show an excess.
  • The 2026 room is entered, not derived. Enter it after any carryforward and re-participation room, within the lifetime limit; the 2027 room is calculated from it with the rules above.
  • One withdrawal, made after that month’s contributions. Several withdrawals, designated transfers to an RRSP or RRIF, and qualifying withdrawals for a home are not modelled.
  • Income tax is a flat estimate. A taxable withdrawal is priced at your entered marginal rate; withholding at source and the effect on benefits are not shown.
  • Eligibility and deadlines. The maximum participation period, account closure and the year after a first qualifying withdrawal end the ability to contribute and are not checked.
  • Penalties and interest on a late RC728 are not included.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 27 October 2026. The first chart shows CRA’s First Home Savings Account Statistics for the 2024 tax year (published 14 October 2026; data processed to 30 June 2026). The other three apply sections 207.01 and 207.021 of the Income Tax Act (current to 30 September 2026) and CRA’s FHSA pages, reviewed 27 October 2026, to hypothetical editable inputs for 2026 and 2027. Investment growth, qualifying withdrawals, account closure, the end of the maximum participation period, penalties and interest are not included. These are planning estimates, not CRA’s assessment. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Justice Laws · Income Tax Act, section 207.021 (tax payable on excess FHSA amount) ↗

    Act current to 30 September 2026; reviewed 27 October 2026. For each month with an excess FHSA amount at any time, tax of 1% of the highest such amount in that month.

  2. Justice Laws · Income Tax Act, section 207.01 (definitions: excess FHSA amount, designated amount) ↗

    Act current to 30 September 2026; reviewed 27 October 2026. Excess FHSA amount = A + B + C − D − E − F; a designated amount may not exceed the excess FHSA amount when designated.

  3. Justice Laws · Income Tax Act, section 146.6 (annual FHSA limit, FHSA carryforward, maximum participation period) ↗

    Act current to 30 September 2026; reviewed 27 October 2026. Annual FHSA limit uses CAD 8,000 plus the FHSA carryforward, which is at most CAD 8,000 and nil before the maximum participation period starts.

  4. Canada Revenue Agency · What happens if you contribute or transfer too much to your FHSAs ↗

    Page details dated 2 February 2026; reviewed 27 October 2026. 1% per month on the highest excess in the month; reduced by new room on 1 January or by designated or taxable withdrawals, designated transfers and deemed income; designated amounts on Form RC727; RC728 with Schedule A; worked examples (Ridwan, Cole, Carolyn and others).

  5. Canada Revenue Agency · Participating in your FHSAs ↗

    Page details dated 17 September 2026; reviewed 27 October 2026. Room formula with unused re-participation room, CAD 8,000 plus participation room carryforward and the CAD 40,000 lifetime limit; examples Karla (2027 room CAD 3,000), Julie (CAD 11,000) and Tony (CAD 9,500, re-participation room CAD 1,500).

  6. Canada Revenue Agency · FHSA taxes payable, assessments and reassessments ↗

    Page details dated 2 February 2026; reviewed 27 October 2026. RC728 and payment due by 30 June of the following year; penalty and interest if late; waiver of the excess tax on Form RC729; penalties and interest through Form RC4288.

  7. Canada Revenue Agency · First Home Savings Account Statistics (2024 tax year), Tables 1 and 2 ↗

    Page details dated 14 October 2026; data processed to 30 June 2026. Canada: 1,455,280 holders, 1,680,490 accounts, 1,038,540 holders who contributed CAD 6,470,717 thousand. Counts rounded to 10, dollars to the thousand. CSV SHA-256 recorded in the editorial notes.
